gloss_terse: to be firm, strong, enduring; used of prosperity and ways that remain stable
gloss_readable: This rare verbal root expresses the idea of being firm or strong, particularly in the sense of enduring or remaining stable over time. It appears only twice, both times describing things that persist: Job's prosperity that does not endure (negated), and the ways of the wicked that are always firm or prosperous. The multilingual evidence points to prosperity and endurance as the core semantic thread, though the French 'enfanter' (to give birth) suggests some translators saw a connection to labor or travail, possibly confusing this root with the more common חול (to writhe).

senses.1: The sense of being firm, strong, or enduring appears in both passages. In Job 20:21, the negation indicates that the prosperity of the wicked does not endure or remain firm. In Psalm 10:5, the parallelism suggests stability and success—his ways are always firm, prosperous, or secure. The English and Spanish glosses ('prosper,' 'will endure,' 'Prosperan,' 'durará') capture the nuance of enduring strength rather than momentary firmness.

gloss_terse: Hul, a descendant of Aram listed in the Table of Nations
gloss_readable: Hul appears in the genealogical lists as a son of Aram, grandson of Shem, in the Table of Nations. The name occurs in both Genesis 10 and the parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1, positioned between Uz and Gether among Aram's descendants. As with many names in these ancient genealogies, Hul likely represents both an individual ancestor and the people or region descended from him, though the specific geographic or ethnic identification has been lost to history.

senses.1: The proper name Hul designates one of the sons of Aram in the Semitic branch of Noah's descendants. Both occurrences are in genealogical contexts (Genesis 10:23 and 1 Chronicles 1:17), listing the same four sons of Aram. The multilingual glosses maintain the transliterated form with minor orthographic variation across languages, reflecting the standard practice for biblical proper names that lack clear etymological meaning.

gloss_terse: hole, cavity; used of an asp's den and hiding places where people are imprisoned
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a hole or cavity, whether natural or man-made. In Isaiah 11:8, it refers to the hole of an asp (a venomous snake), part of the prophetic vision of the peaceable kingdom where even infants play safely near dangerous creatures. In Isaiah 42:22, the plural form describes holes or dungeons where people are hidden away as prisoners or plunder. The German confusion with 'young men' likely reflects a scribal or translational error conflating this with בחורים (young men).

senses.1: A hole or cavity, used both literally (the den of a serpent) and metaphorically (prison cells or dungeons). Isaiah 11:8 uses the singular to describe the asp's hole in a context of messianic peace, while Isaiah 42:22 employs the plural in a context of judgment and captivity. The Spanish 'calabozos' (dungeons) in 42:22 helpfully captures the imprisoning function of these holes.

gloss_terse: white (fabric), fine white linen or cotton; a luxurious textile material
gloss_readable: This term refers to white fabric, likely fine linen or possibly cotton, used in royal and luxurious contexts. Both occurrences in Esther describe opulent settings in the Persian court: the palace furnishings in Susa and Mordecai's royal garments. The white material is consistently paired with violet or purple, emphasizing the regal and precious nature of these textiles. BDB notes uncertainty whether the material was cotton or linen, but the context clearly indicates a high-quality white fabric suitable for royalty.

senses.1: White fabric or white stuff, a luxurious textile used in royal settings. In Esther 1:6, it describes the white hangings in the palace of Susa, held with cords of fine linen and purple. In Esther 8:15, it forms part of Mordecai's royal attire alongside violet. The consistent pairing with purple and violet (תכלת) across languages confirms this is a prestigious white material, not simply the color white applied to any object.

gloss_terse: Hauran, a district southeast of Mount Hermon in ancient Syria
gloss_readable: Hauran designates a geographical region southeast of Mount Hermon, extending between Jaulan and Lejah toward the Syrian desert. Ezekiel mentions it twice in his vision of the restored land's boundaries, describing the border of Hauran in relation to Damascus. The name's etymology is uncertain—proposals include 'black land' (referring to the basaltic soil), 'land of caves,' or 'hollow land,' though none can be confirmed. The region was significant in both biblical and post-biblical Jewish history.

senses.1: The territorial name Hauran appears only in Ezekiel 47, defining the northeastern boundary of the restored Israel. Verse 16 mentions 'the border of Hauran,' and verse 18 distinguishes it from Damascus. The multilingual transliterations (Spanish 'Jaurán,' French 'Havran') reflect the known Arabic form حَوْرَان (Ḥawrān), preserving the connection to the historical region that remained significant in later periods.

gloss_terse: Hushim, wife of Shaharaim of the tribe of Benjamin
gloss_readable: Hushim (also spelled Chushim in variant forms) was one of the wives of Shaharaim, a Benjamite whose complex genealogy is recorded in 1 Chronicles 8. The name appears with slight orthographic variation in the two verses, reflecting the common fluidity in Hebrew spelling of proper names. As a female proper name, Hushim is distinct from the male name Hushim associated with the tribe of Dan in Genesis 46.

senses.1: The personal name of Shaharaim's wife in the Benjamite genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8. The name appears in verses 8 and 11 with minor spelling variation (חושים and חשים). The Spanish transliterations 'Jusim' and 'Y-de-Jusim' (and from Jusim) show the name both alone and in construct relationship, while other languages preserve the 'H' sound (Hushim, Chushim).

gloss_terse: Hushim, a son of Dan listed in Genesis 46 and 1 Chronicles 7
gloss_readable: Hushim was a son of Dan according to Genesis 46:23, making him one of Jacob's grandsons who went down to Egypt. The name appears in variant spellings: Hushim in Genesis 46 and 1 Chronicles 7:12, but as Shuham in Numbers 26:42 (where his descendants are called Shuhamites). This kind of orthographic variation is common in biblical genealogies, where the same individual or clan may be recorded with different but related name forms across multiple texts.

senses.1: The proper name of Dan's son in the patriarchal genealogies. Genesis 46:23 records 'the sons of Dan: Hushim' (using the plural form for a single son), while 1 Chronicles 7:12 mentions 'Hushim the sons of Aher.' The connection to Shuham of Numbers 26 is widely recognized by scholars. The multilingual glosses maintain the transliterated form with variations in initial consonant (H/J/Ch) according to language conventions.

gloss_terse: Hotham, the name of two men in the tribe of Asher and among David's warriors
gloss_readable: Hotham is a personal name borne by two different men in the biblical record. The first was a descendant of Asher mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:32 (where he is identified with Helem in verse 35). The second was the father of two of David's mighty warriors listed in 1 Chronicles 11:44. The name appears only in Chronicles and is preserved in various forms in the ancient versions, suggesting some uncertainty about its exact pronunciation.

senses.1: A masculine proper name appearing in Asherite genealogies and Davidic warrior lists. In 1 Chronicles 7:32, Hotham is listed among the sons of Heber in Asher's lineage. In 1 Chronicles 11:44, he is identified as the father of Shama and Jeiel, two of David's valiant men. The Septuagint variations (Χωθαν, Κωθαν) reflect attempts to render an unfamiliar Hebrew name in Greek, while modern translations consistently use Hotham or its equivalent.

gloss_terse: visibility, sight; the visible appearance or extent of the great tree in Nebuchadnezzar's dream
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun, appearing only in Daniel 4, denotes visibility or the extent to which something can be seen. It describes the great tree in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, whose visibility or sight reached to the ends of the earth. The term emphasizes not just the tree's height but its conspicuous, far-reaching presence—visible from every direction. The word appears with a third-person feminine suffix, referring back to the tree (which is feminine in Aramaic).

senses.1: The visible extent or visibility of an object, specifically used of the cosmic tree in Nebuchadnezzar's vision. Daniel 4:11 and 4:20 both use the phrase 'and its visibility (reached) to the ends of all the earth,' emphasizing the universal scope of the tree's appearance. The multilingual glosses ('visibility,' 'visibilidad') consistently capture this sense of being seen or observable across great distances, appropriate to the apocalyptic imagery of the passage.

gloss_terse: Hezir, name of a priest and a leader who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah
gloss_readable: Hezir appears as the name of two post-exilic figures. First, he was a priest who headed the seventeenth priestly course in the divisions established (according to Chronicles) in David's time. Second, he was one of the leaders who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah. The name's etymology is debated—it may be vocalized to avoid offense (avoiding the word for 'swine'), or it may derive from words for pomegranate or apple, as suggested by the Talmudic and Syriac cognates.

senses.1: A masculine proper name of priestly and leadership associations in the post-exilic period. 1 Chronicles 24:15 lists Hezir as the head of the seventeenth priestly division, while Nehemiah 10:20 names him among those who set their seal to the covenant. The Septuagint variations (Ηζειρ, Χηζειρ) show the typical Greek attempts to render the Hebrew name, with both passages maintaining recognizable forms of the name across languages.

gloss_terse: strong, strengthening, growing stronger; Qal participle of חזק used adjectivally
gloss_readable: This adjectival form of the common verb חזק (to be strong, to strengthen) appears in two distinct contexts. In Exodus 19:19, it describes the sound of the trumpet growing continually stronger at Mount Sinai during the theophany. In 2 Samuel 3:1, it characterizes David's house as growing stronger over time in contrast to Saul's weakening house. The participle form captures the dynamic, ongoing nature of the strengthening process rather than a static state.

senses.1: The Qal active participle used as an adjective to describe ongoing or increasing strength. Exodus 19:19 uses it with the conjunction: 'the sound of the trumpet growing continually stronger.' 2 Samuel 3:1 employs it in a political context: David's house growing stronger while Saul's grows weaker. The multilingual evidence shows dynamic verb forms ('fortaleciéndose' - becoming strong, 'strengthening') rather than static adjectives, confirming the participial nature of the Hebrew.

gloss_terse: sin, sin offering; a feminine noun denoting transgression or the sacrifice for it
gloss_readable: This is a common feminine noun for sin, though these two particular occurrences involve textual variants. In Ezekiel 18:21, the Qere (traditional reading) has 'his sins' while the text appears different. In Daniel 9:24, the word refers to sins in the context of the seventy weeks prophecy. The term can denote both the act of sin and the offering made for sin, though in these contexts it refers to moral transgression. The feminine form distinguishes it from related masculine nouns for sin.

senses.1: Sin or transgression as a moral offense. Ezekiel 18:21 speaks of turning away from sins (with a textual note about the Qere reading), while Daniel 9:24 includes 'to finish transgression and make an end of sins' in the prophetic program. The consistent glosses across languages ('sin,' 'pecado,' 'péché,' 'Sünde') confirm this is the standard word for sin, here in specific prophetic and moral contexts involving repentance and divine judgment.

gloss_terse: sinful thing, sin; feminine noun emphasizing the concrete sinful act or condition
gloss_readable: This feminine form denotes sin as a concrete thing or condition, appearing in two significant texts about divine mercy and human wickedness. In Exodus 34:7, it occurs in the proclamation of God's name to Moses, where the LORD declares His forgiveness of iniquity, transgression, and sin. In Isaiah 5:18, it describes those who draw sin with cords as if hauling it along. The noun emphasizes sin as an objective reality or tangible burden.

senses.1: A sinful thing or sin viewed as a concrete entity. Exodus 34:7 lists it among the offenses God forgives ('forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin'), while Isaiah 5:18 uses vivid imagery of people dragging sin with cords like a cart. The multilingual glosses uniformly render it as 'sin' or 'péché,' though the Hebrew feminine form (חטאה) carries slightly different nuance than the more common חטאת—BDB distinguishes this as 'sinful thing' to emphasize its concrete character.

gloss_terse: sin (Aramaic); the Aramaic equivalent of Hebrew חטא with Qere-Ketiv variant
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun for sin appears only in Daniel 4:27, where Daniel urges Nebuchadnezzar to break off his sins by practicing righteousness. The text has both a Qere (traditional reading) and Ketiv (written text) variant, reflecting uncertainty about the precise form—whether חטאך (your sin) or חטיך (alternative spelling). The word is parallel to 'your iniquities' in the same verse, showing it refers to moral offenses that can be remedied through righteous action.

senses.1: Sin or sins in the Aramaic portions of Daniel. The verse appears twice (Daniel 4:27 in English, counted as two entries for the variant readings) with both Qere and Ketiv forms noted. The counsel is to 'break off your sins by righteousness and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed.' All language traditions recognize this as the standard Aramaic word for sin, parallel to Hebrew חטא, shown by the consistent glosses ('sins,' 'pecados,' 'péché,' 'Sünde').

gloss_terse: sin offering (Aramaic); a sacrifice offered for atonement
gloss_readable: This Aramaic term designates a sin offering in Ezra 6:17, where the returned exiles offer sacrifices at the dedication of the rebuilt temple. The word appears in both Ketiv and Qere forms (חטיא and חטאה), reflecting variant spellings of the same concept. It corresponds to the Hebrew חטאת when referring to the sacrificial offering rather than the sin itself. The Nabatean cognate חטיאת means 'penalty,' showing the broader Aramaic semantic range of atonement and restitution.

senses.1: A sin offering or sacrifice for atonement in the post-exilic temple dedication. Ezra 6:17 describes offerings made at the dedication: bulls, rams, lambs, and 'male goats for a sin offering for all Israel, twelve according to the number of the tribes.' The verse is listed twice due to the Ketiv-Qere variants in the text. The multilingual evidence ('sin offering,' 'expiación,' with textual notes) confirms this is the sacrificial sense, not merely the abstract concept of sin.

gloss_terse: Hatita, head of a Levitical family of gatekeepers who returned from exile
gloss_readable: Hatita was the head of a family of Levitical gatekeepers who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. The name appears in both Ezra 2:42 and the parallel list in Nehemiah 7:45, as part of the registry of those who came back to Jerusalem. As with many names in these post-exilic lists, the exact etymology is uncertain, but the consistent appearance in both genealogical records confirms this was a recognized family of temple servants.

senses.1: The proper name of a Levitical family head in the return from exile. Both Ezra 2:42 and Nehemiah 7:45 list 'the sons of Hatita' among the gatekeepers, with the total count varying slightly between the two parallel accounts (as is common in these lists). The Septuagint transliterations (Ατητα, Ατειτα, Ατιτα) show Greek attempts to render an unfamiliar name, while modern languages maintain recognizable forms (Hatita, Jatitá, Chatita).

gloss_terse: Hattil, head of a family among Solomon's servants who returned from exile
gloss_readable: Hattil was the ancestral head of a family listed among 'the children of Solomon's servants' who returned from Babylonian exile. The name appears in both the Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 lists of returning exiles, specifically among those families descended from royal servants. The designation 'Solomon's servants' likely refers to temple functionaries or administrative personnel associated with the temple complex rather than literal servants of Solomon himself.

senses.1: A masculine proper name appearing in post-exilic genealogical lists. Ezra 2:57 and Nehemiah 7:59 both record 'the sons of Hattil' among the descendants of Solomon's servants. The Septuagint shows significant variation (Αττεια, Αττιλ, Εγηλ, Εττηλ), suggesting uncertainty about pronunciation, but the Hebrew consonantal text remains consistent. Modern languages render it as Hattil, Hatil, Chattil, or Jatil depending on convention.

gloss_terse: Hatipha, head of a Nethinim family who returned from exile
gloss_readable: Hatipha was the head of a family among the Nethinim (temple servants) who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. The name appears in both Ezra 2:54 and Nehemiah 7:56 in the lists of returning exiles. The Nethinim were a class of temple servants, possibly including descendants of foreign peoples dedicated to temple service, who performed various menial tasks associated with worship in the post-exilic period.

senses.1: A personal name designating a Nethinim family head in the restoration period. The parallel passages in Ezra and Nehemiah both list 'the sons of Hatipha' among the temple servants returning from exile. The Septuagint variations (Ατουφα, Ατιφα, Ατειφα) reflect Greek attempts at transliteration, while the modern language forms (Hatipha, Hatifa, Chatifa, Jatifá) follow standard conventions for rendering Hebrew ḥ and ṭ sounds.

gloss_terse: branch, twig, rod; a shoot or staff, used literally and metaphorically
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a branch, twig, or rod, appearing in both literal and figurative contexts. In Isaiah 11:1, it forms part of the famous messianic prophecy: 'A shoot shall come forth from the stump of Jesse,' parallel to 'branch' (נצר). In Proverbs 14:3, it appears in the metaphor 'in the mouth of a fool is a rod of pride,' suggesting that a fool's words become an instrument of his own punishment. The term emphasizes something that grows from or extends out from another.

senses.1: A branch, twig, shoot, or rod. Isaiah 11:1 uses it for the messianic shoot from Jesse's line—a new growth from the seemingly dead stump of David's dynasty. Proverbs 14:3 employs it metaphorically for the 'rod of pride' in a fool's mouth, suggesting his words become the instrument of his downfall. The multilingual glosses show both botanical ('shoot,' 'vara') and instrumental ('rod,' 'staff') meanings, with the context determining the primary sense in each passage.

gloss_terse: Helam, a place east of Jordan where David defeated the Arameans
gloss_readable: Helam was a location east of the Jordan River where David achieved a significant military victory over the Aramean coalition under Hadadezer. The site is mentioned in 2 Samuel 10:16-17, with slight spelling variation between the verses (חילם and חלאמה). Some ancient versions and scholars suggest the word should be read as 'their army' rather than a place name, but most accept it as a geographical location somewhere between Damascus and Hamath. Ezekiel 47:16 may also reference this place, though the text is uncertain.

senses.1: A place name designating a battlefield location east of the Jordan. 2 Samuel 10:16 states that the Arameans gathered at Helam, and verse 17 records that David came to Helam and fought them there. The Septuagint (Αιλαμ) supports reading this as a place name, and the reference in Ezekiel 47:16 (if correctly identified) would place it on the border between Damascus and Hamath. The consistent transliteration across languages (Helam, Jelam) confirms the traditional understanding as a proper noun.

gloss_terse: Hirah, an Adullamite and friend of Judah in Genesis 38
gloss_readable: Hirah was an Adullamite man who appears as Judah's friend in the narrative of Genesis 38. He accompanied Judah to Timnah for the sheepshearing and later was sent to deliver payment to the woman Judah thought was a prostitute (who was actually his daughter-in-law Tamar in disguise). The name's etymology is uncertain, though it may be connected to the root חור. His designation as 'the Adullamite' identifies him with the town of Adullam in the Shephelah region of Judah.

senses.1: The personal name of Judah's Adullamite companion in Genesis 38. Verse 1 introduces 'Hirah the Adullamite,' and verse 12 mentions 'his friend Hirah the Adullamite' accompanying Judah to the sheepshearing. The Septuagint Ειρας shows Greek adaptation of the name, while modern languages maintain forms like Hirah, Jirah, or Chira depending on how they render the Hebrew ḥet.

gloss_terse: Hacaliah, the father of Nehemiah the governor
gloss_readable: Hacaliah was the father of Nehemiah, the cupbearer to King Artaxerxes who became governor of Judah and led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. His name appears twice in the book of Nehemiah, both times as part of Nehemiah's self-identification. The name's etymology is uncertain, though one proposal suggests it means 'wait for Yahweh' (from the root חכה). The Septuagint shows considerable variation in rendering the name, reflecting its unfamiliarity to Greek translators.

senses.1: A masculine proper name, specifically the patronymic of Nehemiah. Nehemiah 1:1 opens with 'The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah,' and Nehemiah 10:1 (10:2 in Hebrew) includes the same identification in a list of those who sealed the covenant. The wide variation in Septuagint forms (Χελκια, Χελκιασ, Αχαλια, Αχελια) suggests scribal uncertainty, but the Hebrew text consistently preserves חכליה.

gloss_terse: Hachmoni, the father of two men associated with David's court
gloss_readable: Hachmoni (meaning 'wise') is a family name or patronymic appearing in two contexts in 1 Chronicles. The first Hachmoni was the father of Jashobeam, one of David's chief warriors and head of the Thirty. The second was the father of Jehiel, who served as tutor or companion to David's sons. Whether these represent the same family or two different families sharing the name is uncertain, but the designation suggests a reputation for wisdom.

senses.1: A proper name functioning as a patronymic or family designation. 1 Chronicles 11:11 identifies Jashobeam as 'son of a Hachmoni, chief of the thirty,' while 1 Chronicles 27:32 mentions 'Jehiel the son of Hachmoni' as being with the king's sons (possibly as their tutor). The name's meaning ('wise one') may indicate a family known for wisdom or learning. Modern languages maintain close transliterations: Hachmoni, Chakmoni, Jacmoní.

gloss_terse: Helah, one of the two wives of Ashur, father of Tekoa
gloss_readable: Helah was one of the two wives of Ashur in the genealogies of Judah. Ashur is called the 'father of Tekoa,' probably indicating he was the founder or leading figure of that town. The name Helah appears twice in 1 Chronicles 4, with her children listed in verse 7. The name's meaning is uncertain (BDB notes 'meaning dub.'), and the Septuagint shows considerable variation in attempting to render it in Greek.

senses.1: A feminine proper name in the Judahite genealogies. 1 Chronicles 4:5 introduces Ashur's two wives, Helah and Naarah, while verse 7 lists 'the sons of Helah: Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan.' The wide range of Septuagint variants (Αωδα, Αοαδα, Αλαα, Ελαα, Ελεα) suggests the Greek translators found this an unfamiliar name. Modern versions consistently use Helah or its equivalent (Jelea, Chel'ah).

gloss_terse: Huldah, the prophetess consulted during Josiah's reign
gloss_readable: Huldah was a prophetess living in Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah. When the book of the Law was discovered in the temple, Josiah sent a delegation to inquire of the Lord through her. Her prophetic oracle confirmed the coming judgment on Judah but promised that Josiah would die in peace before the disaster came. She is one of only a few women explicitly called a prophetess in the Hebrew Bible, and her authority was recognized by the king and high priest alike.

senses.1: The proper name of the prophetess consulted by Josiah. 2 Kings 22:14 and the parallel 2 Chronicles 34:22 both record that the delegation 'went to Huldah the prophetess,' describing her as the wife of Shallum, keeper of the wardrobe, and noting that she lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter. The Septuagint Ολδα shows straightforward transliteration, and modern languages maintain consistent forms (Huldah, Hulda, Juldah, Chuldah).

gloss_terse: Heldai, name of one of David's warriors and a returned exile
gloss_readable: Heldai is a personal name appearing in two contexts: as one of David's mighty warriors and as a returned exile in Zechariah's time. The name shows variation with similar forms (Heled, Heleb) in parallel passages, reflecting the common fluidity in spelling of proper names in biblical texts. In 1 Chronicles 27:15, Heldai is listed as a commander for the twelfth month, while Zechariah 6:10 mentions him among those who brought gifts from Babylon. The name may be related to the root meaning 'worldly' or 'transient.'

senses.1: A masculine proper name borne by two (or possibly the same) individuals. 1 Chronicles 27:15 identifies Heldai the Netophathite as a military commander, while Zechariah 6:10 speaks of 'Heldai' (called Helem in verse 14) as one who brought silver and gold from the exile. The preposition מן ('from Heldai') in Zechariah shows the name in construct relationship. The Septuagint variations and parallel forms (Heled, Heleb) illustrate the typical textual fluidity in proper names.

gloss_terse: ornament, jewelry; precious adornment worn on the body
gloss_readable: This noun denotes ornamental jewelry or precious adornments worn on the body. In Proverbs 25:12, it appears in a comparison: 'Like a gold ring or an ornament of fine gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear.' In Song of Songs 7:1, it describes the beauty of the beloved's graceful movements with jeweled ornaments. The term emphasizes the precious, decorative nature of fine jewelry, whether rings, necklaces, or other body adornments.

senses.1: Ornament or jewelry, particularly fine or precious adornments. Proverbs 25:12 uses the singular in parallel with 'a ring of gold,' specifically 'an ornament of fine gold,' to illustrate the value of wise rebuke. Song of Songs 7:1 employs the plural 'ornaments' (or 'jewels') in describing the beloved's beauty. The multilingual glosses consistently point to precious jewelry or ornamental objects ('ornament,' 'joyas,' 'joyaux'), with the context determining whether the reference is to a single piece or multiple adornments.

gloss_terse: armor, equipment, spoil; what is stripped from a person as plunder in war
gloss_readable: This noun refers to equipment, armor, or spoils stripped from someone in battle. It appears only with possessive suffixes, always denoting what is taken from defeated enemies. In Judges 14:19, Samson takes the garments of thirty Philistines he killed. In 2 Samuel 2:21, Joab's brother Asahel is told to seize the armor of one of the young men instead of pursuing Abner. The term emphasizes the military context of plundering the defeated.

senses.1: Armor, equipment, or spoils stripped from enemies in warfare. Judges 14:19 uses 'their equipment' (what Samson took from the thirty men he struck down to pay his wager), while 2 Samuel 2:21 has 'his armor' (the equipment Asahel could have taken from a younger warrior). The multilingual glosses show both the military gear sense ('armor,' 'armure,' 'Rüstung') and the plunder aspect ('spoil,' 'despojo,' 'despojos'), reflecting the dual nuance of equipment taken as war booty.

gloss_terse: to play the pipe, to pipe; denominative verb from the word for flute
gloss_readable: This denominative verb, derived from the noun for flute or pipe (חליל), means to play the pipe or flute. It appears in two celebratory contexts: Solomon's coronation in 1 Kings 1:40, where the people piped with pipes in joyful celebration, and Psalm 87:7, which mentions both singers and pipe-players (or possibly dancers, as the form is ambiguous and could also derive from the root meaning to dance). The verb captures the festive, musical atmosphere of celebration.

senses.1: To play the pipe or flute in celebration. 1 Kings 1:40 describes the people's response to Solomon being anointed: 'and the people piped with pipes and rejoiced with great joy.' Psalm 87:7 mentions 'as well the singers as the pipe-players,' though some interpret this as 'dancers' from a different root. The Assyrian cognate ḫâlalu supports the meaning of pipe-playing, and the context in both passages is festive celebration with music.

gloss_terse: to be healthy, strong; to become strong or restore to health
gloss_readable: This verb means to be or become healthy and strong. It appears in Job 39:4, describing wild animals' young that grow strong in the open field, and in Isaiah 38:16, where Hezekiah asks God to restore him to health. The root is common in cognate languages (Aramaic, Syriac) with the sense of healing and strengthening. The Hiphil form in Isaiah carries the causative sense: 'make me healthy, restore me to health.'

senses.1: To be or become healthy and strong. Job 39:4 uses the Qal imperfect: 'Their young ones become strong (or healthy), they grow up in the open field.' Isaiah 38:16 employs the Hiphil: 'restore me to health and make me live,' parallel to 'make me live.' The multilingual glosses sometimes confuse this with חלם 'to dream' (French 'rêver'), but the context clearly supports health and strength. Spanish 'Se fortalecen' (they become strong) and 'me sanarás' (you will heal me) accurately capture the meaning.

gloss_terse: in exchange for, in return for; used as a preposition indicating compensation
gloss_readable: This term functions as a preposition meaning 'in exchange for' or 'in return for,' derived from a noun meaning 'exchange.' It appears twice in Numbers 18, both times specifying what the Levites receive in exchange for their service in the tabernacle. The Aramaic cognates (חלף, ܚܠܳܦ) are commonly used with the same prepositional sense, showing this is a standard term for indicating compensation or substitution.

senses.1: In exchange for, in return for—a preposition indicating compensation or payment for service rendered. Numbers 18:21 states that God gives the Levites the tithe 'in return for their service that they serve, the service of the tent of meeting,' and verse 31 repeats 'in exchange for your service in the tent of meeting.' The consistent multilingual rendering ('in exchange for,' 'a cambio de,' 'in tauschen für') confirms the prepositional, compensatory sense.

gloss_terse: Helek, a Gileadite clan founder listed among Manasseh's descendants
gloss_readable: Helek (meaning 'portion') was a descendant of Gilead in the genealogies of Manasseh. He is listed among the clans of Manasseh who received territorial allotments in the conquest of Canaan. Numbers 26:30 mentions him in the wilderness census among Gilead's sons, and Joshua 17:2 lists him among the clans receiving inheritance west of the Jordan. As with many such names, Helek likely represents both an individual ancestor and the clan descended from him.

senses.1: A personal and clan name in the Manassite genealogies. Numbers 26:30 lists 'of Helek, the clan of the Helekites,' while Joshua 17:2 specifies the inheritance 'for the sons of Helek' among other Manassite clans. The Septuagint shows variations (Χελεγ, Κελεζ, Ελεκ), but the name is consistently preserved. Modern languages maintain the transliterated form with the preposition indicating relationship: 'to/of/for Helek.'

gloss_terse: the smooth, the bare (mountain); a proper name for a mountain or range
gloss_readable: This adjective-turned-proper-name designates a mountain or mountain range marking the southern limit of Joshua's conquests. The phrase 'the bare (or smooth) mountain' appears twice in Joshua as a geographical marker. Scholars have proposed two possible identifications: either white limestone cliffs about eight miles south of the Dead Sea, or Mount Mâdara southwest from the Pass es-Ṣafâ. The name emphasizes the mountain's smooth or bare character, perhaps referring to its lack of vegetation or its white, exposed rock.

senses.1: A geographical designation, 'the bare mountain' or 'the smooth mountain,' functioning as a proper name. Joshua 11:17 describes the extent of Joshua's conquests 'from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir,' and Joshua 12:7 repeats the same boundary marker. The article in Hebrew ('the bare' or 'the smooth') suggests this was a descriptive name that became a fixed toponym. Most translations render it as 'Mount Halak' or simply 'Halac,' treating it as a proper noun.

gloss_terse: Helkath, a Levitical city in the territory of Asher
gloss_readable: Helkath (meaning 'portion' or 'possession') was a town in the tribal territory of Asher, later assigned to the Levites. It appears in the boundary description of Asher in Joshua 19:25 (spelled חלקת) and in the list of Levitical cities in Joshua 21:31 (spelled חלקת). The two different spellings represent minor orthographic variants of the same place name, a common phenomenon in biblical geographical lists. The exact location is uncertain, though it was somewhere in Asher's allotment.

senses.1: A place name designating a Levitical city in Asher. Joshua 19:25 includes 'Helkath' among the cities in Asher's border description, while Joshua 21:31 lists 'Helkath with its pasturelands' as one of the cities given to the Levites from Asher. The Septuagint variations (Ελεκεθ, Χελκατ, Ελκαθ, Θελκαθ) show Greek attempts to render the name, while modern versions use Helkath, Helcat, or Chelqath, maintaining the consonantal root.

gloss_terse: Helkath-hazzurim, the field of swords/flints; site where Ishbosheth's men fell
gloss_readable: Helkath-hazzurim (literally 'field of the swords' or 'field of the flints/edges') was the name given to a location near the pool of Gibeon where twelve men from each side—Ishbosheth's forces and David's—engaged in deadly combat, with each man grabbing his opponent and thrusting his sword into his side, so that all twenty-four fell together. The name appears twice in 2 Samuel 2:16 as both the place name and its explanation. The etymology suggests either 'field of sword-edges' or possibly 'field of the plotters/adversaries.'

senses.1: A place name and descriptive designation for the site of a deadly contest at Gibeon. 2 Samuel 2:16 states, 'Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is in Gibeon,' with both occurrences in the same verse. The name combines 'field' (חלקה) with either 'swords/edges' (צרים) or 'plotters/adversaries,' eternally marking the site of this violent encounter. The Septuagint's 'portion of the plotters' (Μέρις τῶν ἐπιβούλων) reflects one interpretation, while modern versions often translate it as 'field of swords' or leave it as a proper name.

gloss_terse: hot, warm; heated by fire or sun
gloss_readable: This adjective describes something hot or warm, heated either by baking or by the sun. In Joshua 9:12, the Gibeonites claim their bread was hot (freshly baked) when they left home, though it has now become dry. In Job 37:17, it describes garments that become hot when the earth is still under the oppressive heat of the south wind. The word emphasizes temperature in both literal contexts—the warmth of fresh bread and the heat retained in clothing.

senses.1: Hot or warm, describing objects heated by baking or atmospheric warmth. Joshua 9:12 uses the masculine singular with 'bread': 'This our bread was hot when we took it,' emphasizing freshness. Job 37:17 employs the masculine plural with 'garments': 'you whose garments are hot when the earth is still because of the south wind.' The multilingual glosses uniformly render the temperature sense: 'hot,' 'warm,' 'caliente,' 'calientes,' confirming this as a straightforward thermal adjective.

gloss_terse: rage, fury (Aramaic); intense anger or wrath
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun denotes rage or fury, appearing only in Daniel 3 in the account of Nebuchadnezzar's anger at Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. The word appears in two forms with slightly different spellings (חמא and חמה), representing the same concept. It describes the king's emotional state when the three Hebrew men refused to worship the golden image. The term corresponds to Hebrew חמה and is cognate with other Semitic words for anger and wrath.

senses.1: Rage, fury, or intense wrath. Daniel 3:13 describes Nebuchadnezzar commanding 'with fury and rage' to bring the three men before him, while 3:19 states that 'the image of his face was changed' and he was 'filled with fury' against them. Both occurrences capture the king's explosive anger at perceived disobedience. The multilingual glosses consistently render it as 'fury' or 'furia,' and the conjunction forms ('and fury,' 'with fury') show it in construct relationship with other terms for anger.

gloss_terse: desirable, precious things; choice objects or garments valued for their worth
gloss_readable: This noun denotes desirable or precious things—objects, garments, or persons valued for their worth and attractiveness. The plural form can refer to choice garments (Genesis 27:15), precious treasures and vessels (Ezra 8:27, 2 Chronicles 20:25), desirable food (Daniel 10:3), or even to persons who are highly valued (Daniel 9:23, 10:11, 10:19). The root sense is 'that which is desired or treasured,' with specific meaning determined by context. The term emphasizes subjective value—what is precious in someone's eyes.

senses.1: Desirable or precious things, whether objects or persons. Genesis 27:15 uses it of Esau's 'choice garments' that Rebekah took for Jacob. Ezra 8:27 employs it for 'precious' vessels 'as precious as gold.' The word can describe valued items (garments, vessels, food) or valued persons (Daniel's designation as a 'precious treasure' or 'greatly loved one'). The multilingual evidence shows both object-focused translations ('preciosos,' 'precious,' 'kostbaren') and quality-focused ones ('desirable,' 'preciados'), capturing the dual nuance of objective worth and subjective value.

gloss_terse: Hammon, a town in Asher or Naphtali, possibly meaning hot spring
gloss_readable: Hammon (possibly meaning 'hot spring') was a town name appearing in two contexts: in the territory of Asher (Joshua 19:28) and in Naphtali (1 Chronicles 6:76, though some identify this with Hammath or Hammoth-dor). The name likely refers to thermal springs in the region, as the root חם relates to heat or warmth. If the two references are to different places, there may have been multiple towns named for local hot springs. The Septuagint and other ancient versions preserve the name with minor variations.

senses.1: A place name in northern Israel, associated with either Asher or Naphtali or both. Joshua 19:28 lists 'Hammon' among the cities in Asher's border, while 1 Chronicles 6:76 (6:61 in Hebrew) mentions it in connection with Naphtali's Levitical cities, possibly identical with Hammath. The etimology suggests 'hot spring,' appropriate for the region. Modern translations maintain the transliterated form: Hammon, Hamón, Jamon, Chammon.

gloss_terse: compassion, mercy, pity; tender feeling that spares from harm
gloss_readable: This noun denotes compassion, mercy, or pity—the tender feeling that moves someone to spare another from harm. Technically an infinitive form from the verb חמל (to spare, have compassion), it functions as a noun in both occurrences. In Genesis 19:16, it describes the LORD's compassion on Lot that led the angels to seize his hand and bring him out of Sodom. In Isaiah 63:9, it appears in parallel with God's love as the motivation for redemption: 'In His love and in His compassion He redeemed them.' The term emphasizes the emotional component of mercy.

senses.1: Compassion, mercy, or pity shown by sparing someone from deserved harm. Genesis 19:16 uses the construct form: 'in the compassion of the LORD upon him,' explaining why the angels forcibly rescued Lot. Isaiah 63:9 pairs it with love: 'in His love and in His compassion He redeemed them,' showing compassion as the emotional motivation for redemptive action. The multilingual glosses ('compassion,' 'pity,' 'compasión,' 'Erbarmen') consistently emphasize the tender, merciful aspect of this divine attribute.
